text: The classical discrete Fourier transform converts a signal from what value at each point in time to how much of each frequency is present. The Quantum Fourier Transform does the analogous job on a quantum state, and it's one of the most important subroutines in quantum computing — Shor's algorithm and quantum phase estimation both use it internally.

You don't need to hand-build the controlled-phase-gate ladder that implements the QFT — core qiskit provides it directly. QFT of num_qubits equals 3 returns a ready-to-use circuit you can append to any larger circuit, or compose with its inverse when you need to undo it.

Mechanically, the QFT takes each computational basis state and maps it to an equal-weighted superposition of all basis states, where each term's phase depends on both the input value and which basis state it is. That phase-depends-on-x property is exactly what lets the output encode information about the input even though every output amplitude has the same magnitude.

Here's the verified behavior for a concrete case. Start with 3 qubits representing decimal 1 — a single sharp spike, probability 1.0 on that one state, zero on the other 7. Apply the 3-qubit QFT, and every one of the 8 basis states now has exactly the same amplitude magnitude, 0.353553, giving every outcome exactly the same measurement probability, 0.125.

But magnitude is only half the story. The |000> term comes out purely real, while the other 7 terms have nonzero imaginary components tracing out a specific phase ramp that depends on the input value. That phase ramp, not the uniform magnitude, is where the information about the input actually lives. Applying a Hadamard to every qubit would also flatten the spike, but with much simpler phase relationships — only the QFT's specific phase ramp is the Fourier-transform relationship that lets you recover frequency information back out.

Next lesson covers algorithms built differently from both Grover and the QFT: variational algorithms, which deliberately split the work between a quantum circuit and a classical optimizer, running back and forth until the result converges.
